catalog_quote: With the exception of a few monosyllabic words that may be unstressed in the sentence, a word has at least one stressed syllable. The primary stress in Livonian is on the first syllable of a word. This is valid also for foreign words. ... If a prosodic word has four or more syllables, the secondary stress is usually on the third syllable of a word
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title: Tuisk 2015 'Livonian word prosody' is the Tartu PhD dissertation (DSpace handle 10062/48857; 54-page summary without appended articles), downloaded open and read. Its p. 31 statement — primary stress on the first syllable, secondary stress usually on the third, -nikā affix exception — confirms the catalog's fixed-strict coding and is a summary of its paper [P4], i.e. the catalog's deciding source Tuisk 2015 LU LI(3):177-195. That article was also downloaded from kirj.ee (open) and the catalog's domain_quote checked verbatim at pp. 177-178 (initial primary stress also in loans; secondary on syllable 3 for 4+ syllables; trisyllabic final secondary foot in odd-length words of 5+; -nikā and late-loan long-vowel exceptions; Latvian-borrowed short verb prefixes unstressed). No contradiction, no refinement beyond what the catalog already flags; nothing left unread; no acquisition priority. Note for the per-language bibliography: item 6 there gives the dissertation as 'Tuisk (2016)'; the record is dated 2015-10-12 (issued 2015). discovery was done via the DSpace REST API, Crossref and Semantic Scholar APIs.

tone_statements.quote: Livonian is the only Finnic language that differentiates two tones in stressed stem-initial syllables. The plain tone is characterised as level or rising and the broken tone or stød as rising-falling. Livonian stød can be defined as a phonological unit, which on the suprasegmental level has particular characteristic features. The most typical aspect is a specific shape of pitch excursion, which sometimes can be accompanied by laryngealization.

tone_statements.citation: Tuisk, Tuuli. 2014. Survey of research on Livonian prosody. Eesti ja soome-ugri keeleteaduse ajakiri / Journal of Estonian and Finno-Ugric Linguistics 5(1): 261-292.
tone_statements.quote: Livonian is the only Finnic language that differentiates two tones in stressed stem-initial syllables. The plain or level tone is characterized as rising and the broken tone or stød as rising-falling. The opposition of the F0 contour in a stressed long syllable is a central phenomenon in Livonian word prosody. In addition to the characteristic tone contour, laryngealization can supervene. ... stød has a phonological role in differentiating meaning, e.g. kallõ ‘island, PSg’, ka’llõ ‘fish, PSg’.
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones (plain=rising, broken/stød=rising-falling, often laryngealized) contrast only in the primary-stressed initial syllable; initial stress stated separately. Survey of acoustic work.

tone_statements.citation: Tuisk, Tuuli. 2012. Tonal and Temporal Characteristics of Disyllabic Words in Spontaneous Livonian. Linguistica Uralica XLVIII(1): 1-11.
tone_statements.quote: The Livonian prosodic system has similarities to that of Estonian as well as Latvian. In Livonian, primary stress is fixed, falling on the first syllable of a word. The tonal system is similar to Latvian. There is a tone opposition in the primary stressed syllable. Like Latvian, Livonian uses stød as one of its prosodic features (for Latvian, cf. Markusa 1991). Words pronounced with stød are often referred to as words with broken tone, and words without stød as words with plain or rising tone.
tone_statements.summary: Two-way tone opposition in the primary-stressed first syllable: broken tone (stød) vs plain/rising tone; fixed initial stress. The paper's own F0 measurements cover only stød-less disyllables.

tone_statements.citation: Tuisk, Tuuli & Pire Teras. 2009. The Role of Duration Ratios and Fundamental Frequency in Spontaneous Livonian. Linguistica Uralica XLV(4): 241-252.
tone_statements.quote: The prosodic features of Livonian are as follows: 1) primary stress is fixed, falling on the first syllable of a word; 2) there is a phonological opposition of short and long primary stressed syllables; ... 3) there is a tone opposition in the primary stressed long syllables (words with stød (or broken tone) and words without stød). ... Stød in Livonian is phonologically contrastive, cf. tī’edõ ’to do’ vs tīedõ ’work (PSg)’, pa’llõ ’to burn’ vs pallõ ’to ask, to beg’. In Livonian transcription, stød is marked with an apostrophe (pū’dõz ’clean’).
tone_statements.summary: Two-way tone opposition (stød/broken tone vs none) only in primary-stressed long syllables; stress fixed initial. F0 study: stød words show early F0 peak; laryngealization in 36% of tokens.

tone_statements.citation: Kuznetsova, Natalia. 2025. The rise of ternary quantity and its alignment with laryngeal articulations. Linguistic Typology 29(2): 319–360. doi:10.1515/lingty-2023-0070
tone_statements.quote: Livonian represents an innovative MULTIPLE Finnic pattern distinguishing between five quantity-stød foot templates. [...] Strong templates, like in Saami, show lengthening or other types of coda strengthening in the stressed syllable (Viitso 2007), including the consonantal Q3 in [ˈkilːˑə], [ˈkitːˑə], or stød, as in [ˈpiˀdːə] or [ˈkuoˀigə]. Like in Saami, Livonian Q3 and stød are restricted to strong templates, so their alignment is SYNERGISTIC. The two features are in complementary distribution across foot structures. Stød is possible in heavy stressed syllables with a long vowel/diphthong/triphthong, or with a short vowel followed by a voiced geminate/cluster.

sources.citation: Tuisk, Tuuli (2015). The Temporal Structure of Livonian Tri-, Tetra- and Pentasyllabic Words. Linguistica Uralica LI(3), 177-195.
sources.quote: With the exception of a few monosyllabic words that may be unstressed in the sentence, a word has at least one stressed syllable. The primary stress in Livonian is on the first syllable of a word. This is valid also for foreign words. Only short-syllable verb prefixes borrowed from Latvian can be unstressed, e.g. no|võ·ttõ 'remove, Inf'. ... If a prosodic word has four or more syllables, the secondary stress is usually on the third syllable of a word (pie·dāgõ:dõn 'pine, DPl'). If a word has five syllables or a larger odd number of syllables, the secondary-stressed foot is usually trisyllabic (o·pāti:jizõn 'teacher, DSg').
sources.note: Primary stress initial (also in loans); secondary stress usually on syllable 3 in words of 4+ syllables; in odd-length words of 5+ syllables the final secondary foot is trisyllabic (10100, 1010100); exceptions: -nikā affix takes secondary stress on syllable 2 'in all cases', late loanwords with a long non-initial vowel can carry secondary stress (ka·ptē:n, be·nzī:n), compounds keep each component's pattern. Verbatim match to the catalog's domain_quote and to its stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 101010 1010100 10101010 (1 = a stressed syllable).

sources.quote: "The prosodic system of Livonian ... is based on syllable weight. The basic foot in these languages is the MORAIC TROCHEE. All these languages also share the undominated constraint that words are stressed on the initial syllable." Confirms initial primary stress; says nothing about the position of secondary stress in 4+ syllable words.

sources.note: First-hand acoustic study (f0 GAMMs + phonation labelling) of the two-way Livonian tonal contrast: broken tone (stød) vs plain tone, contrastive only in (primary-)stressed long syllables (stød-basis = long vowel/diphthong/triphthong or short vowel + voiced geminate/cluster); stød = early rapid f0 rise(-fall), often with non-modal (creaky) phonation; finds the contrast tends to be neutralised in spontaneous speech with speaker and sex differences; research-history section reviews Posti's three-tone (rising/broken/falling) proposal.

tone.quote: The prosodic features of Livonian are as follows: 1) primary stress is fixed, falling on the first syllable of a word; 2) there is a phonological opposition of short and long primary stressed syllables; ... 3) there is a tone opposition in the primary stressed long syllables (words with stød (or broken tone) and words without stød). ... Stød in Livonian is phonologically contrastive, cf. tī’edõ ’to do’ vs tīedõ ’work (PSg)’, pa’llõ ’to burn’ vs pallõ ’to ask, to beg’. In Livonian transcription, stød is marked with an apostrophe (pū’dõz ’clean’).

sources.quote: Unfortunately, not quite enough is known about Livonian sted whose characteristic like that of the Latvian broken tone (lauzta intonacija) and of Danish sted is a period of laryngealization in the second half of the syllable nucleus. The stress in Livonian cannot be left out of consideration as any formulation of the problems of quantity and sted depends on how one interprets the dynamic stress.
sources.note: First-hand structural phonology: stød (like Latvian lauztā intonācija and Danish stød) = laryngealization in the second half of the syllable nucleus; proposes an accentual analysis of stressed syllables with grave and broken (= stød) accents, later acute and 'drop' accents, nine accent paradigms, so that vowel/consonant quantities are accent-conditioned; section 5 reviews Posti's three-tone (rising, broken, falling) phonologization and argues the falling tone marks a compound boundary, leaving two tones; cites Kettunen 1936-47, Posti 1936-42, Suhonen 1973, Vihman 1971.
